output.brief: The gap is mostly a time-in-level effect, not where people work. Remote hiring only opened widely in July 2024, so 215 of 340 remote staff started after March 2025. Only 32% of remote staff are past the 18-month minimum, against 74% of office staff. Among eligible people, nomination, approval and promotion rates are nearly identical: 20.0% remote against 21.1% office. Applying office rates to the remote eligibility mix predicts 8.2%, against 7.6% observed. Remote staff don't leave more often (10.9% against 11.6%). The gap also shows up within every job family, so job-family mix doesn't explain it. I'm fairly confident, but not certain. The eligible remote group is only 110 people, so a real difference of a few points can't be ruled out. Managers' habit of handing urgent work to whoever is nearby is anecdotal, and I haven't measured it. Don't adopt the three-day office rule. It would penalise people hired on home-based contracts and rest on a misread statistic. Instead, hold the proposal, report promotion rates for eligible employees only, and re-check at the FY2027 cycle. Also measure stretch-assignment allocation, and clarify the promotion criteria for remote staff, since 41% of them say they understand them against 58% of office staff.
